items.paragraph: In places where many people cycle, the risk of injury for each cyclist tends to be lower than in places where few do. This pattern is often read as proof that drivers become more careful when cyclists are common, so that simply encouraging more cycling will make it safer. The pattern is real, but the causal story may run partly the other way. Cities that have built protected lanes and calmed their traffic attract more cyclists precisely because cycling there is already safer, and more cautious people take up cycling only when it feels safe. Driver adaptation may contribute as well; nobody needs to deny it. What the pattern does not support is the hope that numbers alone, without the infrastructure that draws them, will deliver safety.

items.paragraph: When a bereaved person is still unable to work or sleep months after a death, there is a growing tendency to describe the condition as a disorder and to offer treatment. In practice the alternative is often neglect: a person whose grief has hardened into years of isolation may receive nothing, because friends have stopped asking and no institution recognises the need. A label can be misused, and grief that is merely intense should not be hurried. Yet a name can also be what makes help available to the minority for whom mourning has stopped moving.

items.paragraph: Many people believe there is a moral difference between telling a lie and saying something true that is designed to mislead. Whatever difference remains seems to lie less in the harm done to the listener than in what the speaker permits himself: a rule against outright falsehood that he keeps even while evading its purpose.

items.paragraph: Translators of rhymed poetry are usually said to face a simple choice between sound and sense. Keep the rhymes, and the translator must bend the meaning to find English words that chime; keep the meaning, and the poem arrives in prose broken into lines. items.paragraph: Seismologists distinguish between predicting an earthquake and forecasting one, and public discussion often blurs the two. A prediction would name a place, a window of days or weeks and a magnitude, precisely enough to justify evacuating a city. A forecast is more modest: it estimates the probability of a strong quake in a region over years or decades, using the record of past ruptures and the strain measured on faults. A forecast cannot tell anyone to leave on Tuesday, but it can tell a city how strict its building codes should be and where a hospital ought not to be built. Judged as failed predictions, forecasts look useless; judged as what they are, they are among the most practically valuable things the science produces.

items.paragraph: Gossip has a poor reputation: it is condemned as idle, malicious and a waste of time. A more sympathetic view, now common among those who study small communities, holds that gossip performs a social function, spreading knowledge of who can be trusted and deterring cheats who fear for their reputations. This view is a useful corrective, but it can slide into a defence of gossip as such. The same mechanism that deters the cheat also punishes the nonconformist, the newcomer and anyone whose private life departs from local expectation, and it does so without a hearing. To say that gossip enforces norms is to say nothing yet about whether the norms deserve enforcing, or whether those it targets had any chance to answer.

items.paragraph: For years it was widely accepted that self-control draws on a limited resource, so that resisting one temptation leaves a person less able to resist the next. The idea was supported by many small experiments and fitted the everyday experience of feeling worn out after a demanding day. When the effect was retested in large studies run to a common plan across many laboratories, it proved much smaller than the earlier work had suggested, and in some cases indistinguishable from zero. It would be too quick to conclude that people never tire of exercising self-control. What the episode shows is that a stack of small studies, each published because it found an effect, can make a weak or absent phenomenon look established, and that agreement with everyday experience is no substitute for a test designed in advance.

items.paragraph: Whether listening to an audiobook counts as reading is usually argued as a question of status, with defenders insisting that the story reaches the mind either way and sceptics treating listening as a lesser substitute. Both sides tend to miss what actually differs. For narrative of moderate difficulty, a competent listener appears to follow and remember the story about as well as a reader does, so the sceptic's claim that listening is shallower is hard to sustain as a general rule. The difference lies in control. A reader sets the pace, slows down at a difficult sentence, glances back to check who said what, and lets the eye run ahead; a listener receives the text at the narrator's speed and must make an effort to go back. For a thriller this hardly matters. For a dense argument, where comprehension depends on rereading, it may matter a great deal. The useful question is therefore not whether listening is reading, but what kind of text is being taken in.

items.paragraph: City authorities often treat street vendors as a nuisance to be cleared: they block pavements, avoid taxes and make a district look disorderly. Each charge contains some truth, but together they describe vendors only from the point of view of those who drive past them. For the office cleaner who needs a cheap meal at six in the morning, or the migrant who cannot yet afford a shopfront, the stall is part of how the city works. Vendors also keep streets watched and lit after shops close, a service no budget pays for. None of this means pavements should belong to whoever claims them first; pedestrians have rights too. It means that regulation which begins from the goal of removal will usually destroy more than it orders, whereas regulation that begins from accommodation can address congestion without abolishing a livelihood.

items.paragraph: Firms that screen job applications with software trained on the records of past hires often defend the practice as more objective than human judgement, since the program applies the same rule to every applicant and cannot be swayed by a candidate's charm. Consistency, however, is not the same as fairness. A program that learns which applicants were hired in the past learns whatever preferences shaped those decisions, including any unjustified ones, and then applies them with perfect regularity. Human recruiters are inconsistent, but their inconsistency at least leaves room for a manager to notice and correct a pattern; a rule embedded in software may go unexamined precisely because it looks impartial.

Parents with regular working hours, enough money and a calm home find shared meals easier to arrange, and those same conditions help children in many other ways. items.paragraph: Teachers are now widely advised to praise children for effort rather than for cleverness, on the reasoning that a child told she is clever may avoid hard tasks for fear of disproving it, while one praised for trying learns that ability grows with work. Praise for effort that is given regardless of outcome can teach a child that trying is what counts even when the method is hopeless, and children are quick to notice when 'good effort' is offered as consolation for failure. What seems to matter is less the word used than whether praise connects what the child did to what resulted, so that the child learns which kinds of effort work.

items.paragraph: Every widely used piece of software eventually discovers that its users depend not only on what it was designed to do but on what it happens to do. A function that returns results in a particular order, though the documentation never promised any order, will sooner or later be relied upon by someone's program. Fixing such behaviour, or merely changing it for good reasons, then breaks that program, and from the user's side a fix that breaks things is indistinguishable from a bug. (1) Maintainers of mature systems therefore end up preserving accidents alongside intentions, and the line between the two blurs with each release. (2) The cost is not only the effort of carrying old behaviour forward. Each preserved quirk constrains the design of everything built later, so that a system's newest parts are shaped by decisions nobody remembers making. (3) Some projects try to escape this guesswork by announcing in advance which behaviours are guaranteed and declaring the rest open to change, a policy that is honest but only partly effective. Users rarely read such declarations, and a change that breaks enough of them tends to be reversed, whatever the policy said. (4)

items.paragraph: It is often said that the ease of digital photography has cheapened the photograph: when a picture costs nothing, people take thousands and look at almost none. The complaint has force, but it assumes that a photograph's value lies in being kept and contemplated. Many of today's pictures do a different job. They are taken to be sent, as a way of saying 'here I am' or 'look at this', and their purpose is fulfilled the moment they are seen, much as a spoken remark is not diminished by being forgotten. What has declined is not the photograph's worth but the share of photographs meant to be kept, and the real loss, if there is one, falls on that smaller group, which now lies buried among the rest.

items.paragraph: Firms that have experimented with a four-day working week at unchanged pay frequently report that output holds steady while staff are happier and less likely to leave. These results are encouraging, but they come with a caution that is easy to overlook. The firms that volunteer for such trials tend to be ones whose managers already expect them to succeed, and whose work, often office-based and flexible, can be compressed by cutting meetings and idle time. A hospital ward, a bus route or a factory line that runs continuously cannot squeeze five days of cover into four by working more efficiently; it needs more people. The trials show that many jobs contain more slack than was supposed, not that the shorter week can be adopted everywhere at no cost.

items.paragraph: Critics of ghostwriting say that a memoir written by someone other than its named author deceives readers, who believe they are reading the subject's own words. The charge assumes a convention that many readers do not share. Few people who buy the autobiography of a famous athlete suppose that the athlete sat alone composing sentences; what they expect is that the story, the opinions and the memories are genuinely the athlete's, and that he or she has approved the result. Measured against that expectation, a ghostwritten memoir deceives only when the content is invented or the subject has not endorsed it. Where readers do expect sole authorship, as with a novel or a scholarly article, concealed ghostwriting remains a real deception.

items.paragraph: It seems obvious that an operation cannot work by suggestion: the knife either repairs the tissue or it does not. For this reason, many surgical procedures entered routine use on the strength of surgeons' observations that their patients felt better afterwards. But patients who undergo surgery also receive attention, hope and a period of rest, and their symptoms often fluctuate and improve on their own. When some procedures have been tested against sham operations, in which patients are anaesthetised and given an incision but the key step is omitted, the improvement in the two groups has turned out to be similar. Such trials raise real ethical questions, since the sham group bears risk without the prospect of direct benefit. Yet without them, it is hard to know whether an operation helps because of what the surgeon does or because of everything that surrounds it.

items.paragraph: Moral rules such as 'do not lie' or 'keep your promises' are often attacked by pointing to exceptions: surely one may lie to save a life, or break a trivial promise to help someone in danger. If a rule has exceptions, the argument runs, it was never really a rule, and we should simply weigh consequences case by case. But the existence of exceptions shows less than this suggests. A rule can be a strong presumption, one that sets the burden of argument and holds unless something weighty overrides it, and such presumptions are valuable precisely because case-by-case weighing is slow, prone to self-serving bias and impossible for others to rely on. Someone who keeps promises only when calculation favours it is not a person others can plan around. The exceptions show that rules are not absolute; they do not show that rules are dispensable.

When a new motorway cuts the journey, many households eventually move further out, to larger and cheaper homes, until the commute is roughly as long as it was before. The investment is not wasted: people gain space and a wider choice of jobs and housing. But its benefit arrives as a larger city rather than as the shorter commute that was promised.

items.paragraph: Most people feel that they would be obliged to help a stranger in danger in front of them, yet feel no comparable obligation to help a stranger in equal danger on another continent. Some philosophers conclude that this feeling is simply a bias: distance, they argue, cannot by itself make a moral difference, so our duties to the distant are as strong as our duties to the near. The argument is powerful, but it moves too quickly. Distance usually travels with other features that may matter, such as whether one is uniquely placed to help, whether one's help will actually arrive, and whether many others could help equally well. To show that the feeling is mere bias, one must show that it survives when these features are held constant, and that is harder than the argument assumes.

options.A: Rules constitute a game, yet obeying their letter does not settle fairness, since a legal move can empty the contest, though the game's spirit is itself read from the rules.

items.paragraph: It is tempting to think of the rules of a game as fences around an activity that exists without them, but moving a bishop diagonally is not a restriction on some freer way of moving a carved piece; outside the rules there is no bishop to move. Rules in this sense constitute a game rather than regulate it. From this some infer that whatever the rules permit is fair, and that a player who finds a loophole has simply played well. The inference is too quick. Rules are written to make a particular contest possible, and a move that satisfies their letter while dissolving that contest, such as a team deliberately losing to secure an easier opponent later, keeps the form of the game while emptying it. Still, the spirit of a game is no free-floating ideal that referees may invoke at will; it can only be read from the contest the rules were built to create, which is why the usual remedy for such an exploit is a better-drafted rule rather than an appeal to conscience.

items.paragraph: Before printing, a language written across a wide region existed in many local forms: scribes spelled as they spoke, and a manuscript copied in one town might look foreign in another. Printing changed the economics of this variety. A printer selling thousands of copies wanted a form of the language that readers across the whole market could follow, and once a few presses settled on particular spellings and grammar, every later book that followed them reinforced the choice. Standard written languages owe at least as much to this commercial pressure as to the decrees of scholars or rulers. The standard that emerged was not necessarily the most elegant or the most widely spoken variety; it was often simply the one used where the presses happened to cluster, and the dialects of other regions came to look like departures from a norm that was partly an accident of trade.

options.B: Chain restaurants tend to cluster along highways and near railway stations, while independent cafes are found more commonly in the quieter residential neighbourhoods of most towns and cities.
options.C: Franchises thrive among passing strangers because uniformity makes their quality predictable, while independents do better with returning locals who can learn which kitchens are good.
options.D: Franchised restaurants generally serve better food than independent cafes do, which explains why travellers so often choose them along highways and near stations.

items.paragraph: A traveller who eats at a franchised restaurant in an unfamiliar town is buying something an independent cafe cannot easily offer: the assurance that the meal will be much like the one eaten at the same chain elsewhere. The independent may cook far better, but the stranger has no way of knowing that in advance, whereas the franchise's sameness is precisely what makes its quality knowable. This is why chains cluster along highways and near stations, where most customers are passing through, while independent places flourish more often in neighbourhoods whose residents return often enough to learn which kitchens are good. Uniformity, so often mocked, is less a failure of taste than an answer to the problem of buying from strangers.

options.A: Asking people to explain step by step how something works is the best way to teach them how everyday devices such as zips and toilets function.
options.B: People pretend to understand everyday devices in order to avoid appearing ignorant, and they admit the truth only when they are forced to explain in detail how the devices actually work.
options.C: Most people understand facts such as capital cities better than they understand machines, because facts are simpler to learn than the workings of devices.
options.D: People overrate their grasp of how things work because familiarity feels like understanding; trying to explain exposes the illusion, which is weaker where knowledge is self-tested.

items.paragraph: Ask people how well they understand how a zip, a flush toilet or a bicycle works, and most will rate their understanding highly. Ask them then to explain, step by step, how the device actually works, and many find they cannot; when asked to rate their understanding again, they mark it down. The confidence was not a lie but a confusion: familiarity with using something, and knowing that an explanation exists somewhere, feels from the inside like possessing the explanation. Notably, the gap is narrower for facts and procedures, such as the names of capital cities or how to tie a knot, where people can check their knowledge by trying to recall or perform it.

items.paragraph: Few school reforms are as popular with parents and teachers as smaller classes. (1) The appeal is intuitive: with fewer pupils, a teacher should be able to notice each child's difficulties and respond to them. (2) The evidence, however, is more mixed than the enthusiasm suggests. Modest cuts, from thirty-two pupils to twenty-eight, say, seem to change little, perhaps because teachers carry on teaching in exactly the way they did before. (3) Larger cuts can help, particularly for the youngest children, but they are expensive and require many new teachers, some of whom will be less experienced than those already in post. The same money might in some cases do more good if it were spent on improving the teaching that pupils already receive. (4)

items.paragraph: A very large volcanic eruption can throw enough fine particles into the upper atmosphere to dim sunlight across much of the globe for a year or more. (1) Summers in the following seasons may turn cold and wet, frosts may arrive out of season, and harvests far from the volcano can fail. It is natural to read the famines that sometimes follow such events as simple consequences of the weather. (2) The historical record suggests a more complicated picture. Regions that suffered similar losses of crops often fared very differently, depending on whether grain could be moved from places that had a surplus, whether stores had been kept and whether authorities acted quickly or hoarded. (3) As a result, the same cold summer could mean hardship in one valley and mass death in the next. (4)

options.A: Corporate jargon shows that the managers who rely on phrases such as 'circling back' usually have nothing of real substance to say to their staff.
options.B: Firms often announce the closure of a department as a 'realignment', so that nobody has to state plainly that people will lose their jobs.
options.C: Corporate jargon is less empty than evasive, sparing speakers from stating unwelcome facts, which makes it worse than its mockers think, since listeners must decode it.
options.D: Critics who mock corporate jargon overstate its harm, since phrases that merely blur unwelcome news serve useful purposes and waste very little of anyone's working time.

items.paragraph: Corporate jargon is usually mocked as empty: phrases about 'leveraging synergies' and 'circling back' are taken to show that those who use them have nothing to say. The mockery misses what the vocabulary does. Much of it serves to soften or blur, so that a decision to close a department can be announced as a 'realignment' without anyone having to state plainly that people will lose their jobs. Such language is not empty but evasive, and evasion has uses for the speaker. This makes it more troubling than the critics allow, not less: an empty phrase merely wastes time, whereas an evasive one shifts the burden of understanding onto listeners, who must work out for themselves what is being done to them.

items.paragraph: Long before electricity carried messages, France in the 1790s began building chains of hilltop towers whose movable arms could be set in many distinct positions, each standing for a letter, word or phrase. An operator watched the neighbouring tower through a telescope, copied its signal and passed it on, so that a message could cross the country far faster than any rider. (1) The system was impressive, but its limits were as instructive as its speed. (2) It worked only in daylight and in clear weather, and every tower needed trained staff who did nothing but watch and repeat. Above all, it was built to serve the state, which saw in rapid communication a means of holding a large territory together. (3) Private citizens were generally not permitted to send messages on it, and the network was never meant to become a public service. (4)

options.A: People usually compare themselves with those who are worse off, which motivates them to work harder and keeps them content even when their own incomes fall.
options.B: Comparing oneself with others is always harmful, since it makes even prosperous people dissatisfied, so people should judge their lives by absolute standards of wealth alone.
options.C: Since people measure themselves against those slightly better off, contentment depends on whom they compare with; such comparison can motivate but, when constant, breeds discontent.
options.D: A worker whose pay increases may still feel poorer than before if the neighbours living around her are receiving larger increases each year than her own.

items.paragraph: People rarely judge their own situation in isolation; they compare it with that of others, and the others they choose are usually those slightly better off. Such upward comparison can motivate, since a colleague who is a little more skilled shows what is within reach. But when the comparison is constant and the gap seems fixed, it breeds dissatisfaction even among people who are doing well by any absolute measure. A worker whose salary rises may feel poorer if her neighbours' salaries rise faster. Contentment, on this account, depends less on what one has than on whom one measures oneself against.

options.A: Radio commentators describe play constantly since listeners cannot see it, while television commentators say less and add what the picture lacks; each suits its audience.
options.B: Radio commentary is more skilful than television commentary, since describing every movement of play demands far greater talent than adding a few occasional remarks.
options.C: Television commentators often use their words to add information such as a player's record, a tactical change or the significance of the moment.
options.D: Television commentators speak less than radio commentators mainly because broadcasters wish to reduce their costs by shortening the spoken commentary on all televised matches.

items.paragraph: Radio and television commentary on the same match sound strikingly different. The radio commentator must describe almost everything: where the ball is, who has it, which way the play is moving, because the listener has no other way of knowing. The television commentator, whose audience can see all this, would be tiresome doing the same, and so speaks less, leaving silences and using words to add what the picture cannot show, such as a player's record, a tactical change or the significance of the moment. Each style is a response to what its audience already possesses.

options.A: Loyalty programmes are mainly a way for shops to reward their regular customers with discounts, out of gratitude for their continued custom over time.
options.B: Loyalty schemes chiefly serve sellers by making it costlier for customers to switch, while also gathering purchase data, even if many customers benefit from them too.
options.C: Shops use the information collected through loyalty cards to find out what their customers buy and how often, and then send them targeted offers.
options.D: Loyalty programmes trick customers into paying more than they otherwise would, so shoppers who join them always end up worse off than those who do not.

items.paragraph: Loyalty programmes look like a gift: buy nine coffees and the tenth is free. For the seller, the point is less the discount than the switching cost it creates. A customer who is halfway to a reward has a reason to return to the same shop even when another is closer or cheaper, because going elsewhere means abandoning the progress already made. The programme also gives the seller information about what customers buy and how often, which can be used to target offers. Customers are not necessarily fooled; many value the rewards and would shop in the same place anyway. But the programme is designed mainly to make leaving a little more expensive than staying.

options.A: Guide users' longer visits show they are not hurrying but support less than deeper engagement, since self-selection and the gap between time and attention weaken that inference.
options.B: Because visitors with audio guides spend longer in the galleries, museums can be confident that the guides deepen their engagement with the works on display.

items.paragraph: Museums that track visitors often find that those using audio guides spend longer in the galleries than those without, and this is readily taken as proof that the guides deepen engagement. The figure deserves a second look. Visitors who choose to rent a guide may already be the more interested ones, so the longer visits might have occurred anyway. And time is an uncertain measure of attention: a visitor can stand before a painting for the full length of a recorded commentary while looking at the floor, listening rather than seeing. The finding is not worthless, since it shows at least that guided visitors are not hurrying through, but it supports a weaker claim than the one usually drawn from it.

items.paragraph: For many people, work supplies far more than an income: it gives the day a shape, provides a circle of colleagues and answers the question of what one does. options.A: Residents of cul-de-sacs walk to nearby shops more often than residents of grids, because the absence of through traffic makes walking safer and pleasanter.
options.B: Cul-de-sacs give residents real quiet and safety, but unlike grids they lengthen trips and concentrate traffic on connecting roads, costs its beneficiaries tend not to see.
options.C: Residents prefer cul-de-sacs because children can play safely in quiet streets, which explains why the layout has spread so widely in suburban planning.
options.D: Grid layouts are superior to cul-de-sacs in every respect, since they let walkers and drivers take many different routes and spread the load of traffic across all the streets.

items.paragraph: Two ideas of the residential street compete in suburban planning. The grid connects every street to several others, so drivers and walkers can take many routes and no single road carries the whole load. The cul-de-sac layout, with its looping roads and dead ends, keeps through traffic out, and residents of the closed streets often value the quiet and the safety of children playing outside. The difficulty is that the quiet is bought with distance: a shop a few hundred metres away as the crow flies may be more than a kilometre away by road, so residents drive for trips they might have walked, and the few roads that connect the loops carry heavy traffic. Each layout serves something real; the cul-de-sac simply moves its costs out of sight of those who enjoy its benefits.

options.A: Readability formulas are worthless guides for textbook writers, since the length of the words and sentences in a passage has no bearing at all on how easily students can understand what it says.
options.B: Short sentences make textbooks harder to follow than long ones, so formulas that reward brevity measure the opposite of what makes a text truly difficult.
options.C: Revising textbooks to raise readability scores can backfire, because the scores track surface features, and shortening sentences may strip out the links between ideas that understanding needs.
options.D: Textbooks should be written in long and complex sentences, since students learn more from dense prose that forces them to work out the meaning for themselves.

items.paragraph: A familiar remedy for textbooks that students find hard is to rewrite them in shorter sentences with commoner words, guided by formulas that score a text by the length of its words and sentences. The formulas do measure something, but what makes a passage hard to understand is often not its vocabulary so much as the gaps it leaves for the reader to fill. Cutting one long sentence into three short ones frequently removes the very words, such as because, although and therefore, that told the reader how the ideas were related; the result scores as easier and is harder to follow. None of this means that dense prose is a virtue or that difficult words never obstruct learning. It means that a readability score measures surface features, and a text revised to improve its score can lose the connective tissue on which comprehension depends.

options.A: Explaining how a villain came to commit terrible acts always makes those acts more disturbing, so writers should give every villain a detailed and painful past.
options.B: Readers find sympathetic villains more disturbing than monstrous ones, because such characters remind them that ordinary people like themselves, and not only monsters, are capable of terrible acts.
options.C: Giving a villain an understandable past does not in itself excuse his deeds and may make them more unsettling; the real fault lies in stories that let such a past cancel moral judgement.
options.D: Recent fiction has weakened moral judgement by giving its tyrants sad childhoods, so that readers come to regard evil as mere misfortune rather than wrongdoing.

items.paragraph: A familiar complaint about recent fiction is that its villains have become too sympathetic: give every tyrant a sad childhood, the critics say, and evil dissolves into misfortune. The complaint mistakes explanation for excuse. To show how a person came to do terrible things is not to claim that the things were less terrible; it may make them more disturbing, since it removes the comfort of thinking that such acts belong to monsters unlike ourselves. Where the criticism does land is on stories that use the backstory to settle the moral question, inviting the reader to feel that a painful past cancels the harm done. The fault there is not sympathy but a failure of nerve: the writer has explained the villain and then flinched from judging him.

options.A: Beginners learn best from teachers who know only a little more than they do themselves, since such teachers can still remember clearly what it was like not to understand the subject.
options.B: Experts explain their subjects badly because they care little about beginners and are unwilling to spend the time needed to teach them properly.
options.C: Experts often explain badly because their own understanding makes a beginner's position hard to imagine, a problem overcome by checking what learners grasp, not by knowing less.
options.D: The more a person knows about a subject, the worse a teacher of that subject the person is bound to be, whatever effort is made to explain it.

items.paragraph: A specialist asked to introduce a field to newcomers frequently leaves them more confused than before, and ill will rarely has anything to do with it. Understanding, once gained, erases the memory of what it was like to lack it. So the specialist jumps over steps that now feel self-evident, reaches for terms that have become automatic and misjudges how much time a novice needs to keep up. The mastery that earns someone the right to teach thus hides from that person the view of the subject a newcomer has. The best teachers get round this not by knowing less but by repeatedly testing what their audience has in fact understood.
